The Sea

The sea does not argue.
It folds and unfolds,
a single long breath
counting itself out
against the shore.

Come at it with your questions,
and it answers in salt,
in weather,
in the small bones
of ships it keeps.

Even the moon leans in.
Even the moon is answered.

Leave something on the sand—
a name, a stone, a promise—
and watch how the water
takes it without malice,
without keeping it.

**The Sea**

Salt on the wind, a long gray swell,
the tide comes in and counts the shells
it borrowed from the shore — and takes
them back, and takes them back, and makes
a mirror of the drowning light.

Somewhere past the horizon, deep,
the old ships sleep, the old ships keep
their cargo of the drowned and gone;
the waves do not forget, and drown
no one twice, and never learn to rest.

**The Sea**

The sea does not ask,
and never forgives,
but holds what it is given—
salt, shipwreck, small coins—
and gives it back as weather.

It learns the shape of every shore
and forgets, and learns again.
Nothing stays, nothing is lost;
only the water moves,
and the light moves on it.

The waves arrive already tired,
carrying the moon's long work

Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem, like a person standing in a hallway holding a note that says "give the note to the person behind you, then read yours."

It works because each call handles a little bit of the problem and then passes the rest along, until there's nothing left to do and the answers "unfold" back to the start.
